title: Takeout - Overview
body:
## Position Overview

**Position:** Takeout Station  
**Station:** Back Line Production  
**Shift:** Lunch & Dinner Service (Weekend / High Volume)

## Purpose

Execute all takeout, online, and to-go food orders with speed and accuracy while maintaining strict separation from dine-in production and supporting overall kitchen flow.

## Core Responsibilities

- Prepare all takeout and online food orders
- Execute to-go items from dine-in tickets (to-go portion only)
- Follow all recipes and portion standards
- Maintain organization, speed, and cleanliness during service
- Communicate clearly with front takeout and other stations

## Order Ownership

- The takeout station is responsible for:
- Online orders
- DoorDash orders
- Full takeout food orders (hot items)
- To-go portions of dine-in tickets

## Not Responsible For

- Quarts/pints of sauce
- Meatballs with sauce (to go)
- These items are handled by **Sauce Jack** and sent directly to the front takeout for bagging.

## Station Boundaries

- Spoon and sauté handle **all dine-in food**
- Takeout station handles **all takeout food production**
- Takeout station only prepares the **to-go portion** of dine-in tickets
- No crossover unless directed by chef or lead

## Workflow

- Read full ticket before starting
- Identify all items the station is responsible for
- Prepare all assigned items to spec
- Follow build charts and portion standards
- Double-check order before sending
- Take to front takeout for final bagging of order if slow, if busy put on top rail and they will come get it.

## Communication

- Call orders clearly and loudly when ready
- Respond immediately to front takeout requests
- Communicate delays early—do not wait

## Coordination with Other Stations

- Sauce Jack handles all quarts/pints and sends directly to front takeout
- Front takeout is responsible for final order assembly and accuracy
- Do not assume another station completed an item

## Quality Standards

- Follow recipe builds exactly
- Maintain portion consistency
- Ensure clean, tight packaging
- Keep station organized and stocked
- Do not sacrifice accuracy for speed

## Critical Rules (Non-Negotiable)

- You are responsible for everything on your ticket
- Do not assume another station made an item
- Do not send incomplete or unchecked orders
- Do not cross into dine-in production
- Communicate before problems happen

## Success on This Station Looks Like

- Orders are accurate and complete on first pass
- Tickets move quickly without confusion
- No missing items or callbacks
- Strong, clear communication with front takeout
- Station stays clean and controlled during rush

## Takeout Station Opening SOP

**Position:** Takeout Station  
 **Shift:** Lunch / Dinner (Weekend & High-Volume Service)

- **Service Targets:**  Friday → Ready by 4:00 PM  Saturday → Ready by 11:00 AM  Sunday → Ready by 12:00 PM

## Purpose

Set up and stock the takeout station to full operational readiness to handle all takeout, online, and to-go production efficiently without support from front-line stations.

## START-UP PROCEDURES

### 1. Clock In & Initial Check

- Wash hands and clock in on time
- Check with chef or line lead for:  Specials  86’d items  Expected volume
- Confirm takeout station is open for service

### 2. Heat & Equipment Setup (DO FIRST)

- Turn on burners
- Light and heat sauce bains:  Alfredo bain  Marinara bain
- Set up chaffer with sauces
- Fill and heat boiling water pots (2 total for pasta)
- Set up small pot + strainer for GF pasta

### 3. Meatball Setup (START EARLY)

- Set up 2 meatball pots
- Add prepped raw meatballs (from prep) Fill with water and begin heating
- Ensure both pots are heating immediately

### 4. Pasta Setup

- Hang pasta in sink wells:  Rigatoni (full pan)  Vermicelli (full pan)
- Set up 4–6 strainer baskets
- Set up drip station:  Medium pot under strainer for water runoff
- Ensure water is heating toward boil

### 5. Pull Product

**Freezer (Upright)**

- Meat tortellini  Cheese tortellini  Meat ravioli  Cheese ravioli  Gnocchi

**Cooler (TCS – MUST BE ON ICE)**

- Bolognese meat mix  Demi glaze  Chopped chicken  Chopped sausage  Shrimp
- Place all TCS items in ice pans on prep table

**Prep Table Items**

- Romano cheese  Parsley  Oil (squeeze bottle)  White wine (squeeze bottle)  Butter (cut into pats)  Salt/pepper mix

### 6. Station Setup

- Cutting board set  Chef knife sharp and ready
- Tongs for pasta  Tongs for burners/proteins
- Organize station for flow:  High-use items in reach  Proteins on ice  Sauces hot and accessible

### 7. Sauce & Hot Holding Check

- Alfredo hot and at temp Marinara hot and at temp Meatballs heating properly
- No cold spots in bains  Stir sauces as needed

### 8. Final Readiness Check

- Before service:
- Rig and verm fully stocked  Meatballs hot and ready (2 pots)  Boiling water at temp
- All proteins stocked and on ice  Sauces hot and ready
- Station clean and organized  Tools in place
- Let Middle and Spoon know when you are open

## Opening Standards (Non-Negotiable)

Do not open station without hot water ready

Do not open without both pasta pans stocked

Do not open without 2 meatball pots started

All TCS products must be kept on ice

Sauces must be hot and ready before first ticket

Station must be fully set before service begins

## Takeout Station Service SOP

**Position:** Takeout Station  
 **Shift:** Service (Lunch & Dinner – Weekend / High Volume)

## Purpose

Execute all takeout, online, and to-go food orders efficiently and accurately while maintaining clear station ownership, strong communication, and consistent production flow.

## 1. Station Responsibilities During Service

- Produce all takeout and online food orders
- Execute to-go items from dine-in tickets (to-go portion only)
- Maintain full control of station production
- Keep station stocked, clean, and organized

## 2. Order Management

Read full ticket before starting  
 Identify all items assigned to takeout station

Separate mentally:

- Takeout items (you own)
- Sauce Jack items (quarts/pints – not yours)

Verify modifiers and special instructions

Group similar orders, when possible, for efficiency

## 3. Production Flow

### Pasta Execution

- Reheat pasta using boiling water (rig / verm)  Use strainer baskets properly  Drain fully before plating

Use correct sauce:

- Marinara bain
- Alfredo bain
- Other builds as required

### Proteins & Add-Ons

Cook or heat:

- Chicken
- Sausage
- Shrimp

Use correct tools (burner tongs, etc.)  
 Do not cross-contaminate

### Specialty Items

Pull from freezer as needed:

- Tortellini (meat/cheese)
- Ravioli (meat/cheese)
- Gnocchi

Cook to order

Do NOT produce:

- Seafood linguini
- Lobster ravioli  (these are handled by sauté when applicable)

## 4. Order Completion

Ensure all items on your ticket are complete

Double-check:

- Portions
- Modifiers
- Packaging

If you are slow, take the order to the takeout department or if busy put it on the upper shelf and they will come get it.

## 5. Coordination with Other Stations

- Sauce Jack handles quarts/pints separately
- Do NOT wait on Sauce Jack to complete your ticket
- Front takeout will combine items

If front takeout calls for missing items → respond immediately

## 6. Station Maintenance During Service

- Keep pasta stocked (rig & verm)  Monitor meatball pots (do not run low)  Keep sauces hot and stirred
- Keep TCS items on ice at all times  Refill proteins before running out
- Keep station clean and organized  Wipe down as needed during slow moments

## 7. Speed & Flow

Maintain steady pace—do not rush and make mistakes

- Work ahead when possible:
- Drop pasta early
- Stage multiple orders
- Call for help early if falling behind
- Do not let tickets stack without action

## 8. Quality Control

- Follow recipe builds exactly  Maintain portion consistency
- Ensure clean packaging  No sloppy or rushed builds
- Hot food must be hot  No cold or underheated product

## 9. Communication

Call orders clearly and loudly  
 Respond immediately to front takeout

Communicate:

- Low product
- Delays
- Issues

Do not assume anything—confirm when needed

## Critical Rules (Non-Negotiable)

- You own everything on your ticket
- Do NOT assume another station made an item
- Do NOT send incomplete orders
- Do NOT cross into dine-in production
- Keep all TCS food on ice
- Keep sauces hot and ready
- Communicate before problems happen

title: Takeout - Closing SOP
body:
## Takeout Station Closing SOP

**Position:** Takeout Station  
 **Shift:** Dinner Close (Weekend & High-Volume Service)

## Purpose

Break down, clean, and reset the takeout station efficiently while maintaining full-service capability until the station is officially closed.

## PRECLOSE PROCEDURES

*(Begin when volume slows – do NOT compromise service)*

### 1. Communication

- Check with chef or line lead before starting preclose
- Confirm:  Expected remaining volume  Large orders pending  Cut-off timing for shutdown

### 2. Product Consolidation

- Consolidate sauces:  Combine remaining Alfredo  Combine remaining marinara
- Consolidate proteins (keep on ice):  Chicken  Sausage  Shrimp  Bolognese  Demi glaze
- Discard any unusable or unsafe product

### 3. Reduce Station Footprint

- Remove excess strainer baskets (keep minimum needed)
- Consolidate tools:  Keep only necessary tongs and utensils active
- Clear unused pans and containers

### 4. Light Cleaning (While Open)

- Wipe down prep surfaces
- Keep cutting board clean and rotated if needed
- Remove trash buildup
- Keep floor clear and safe

### 5. Restock for Final Push

- Ensure enough:  Rigatoni  Vermicelli  Sauce levels  Proteins

Do NOT run out before close

### 6. Early Shutdown (Chef Discretion Only)

*(Typically, Fri ~8 PM if slow, Sat 8 PM, Sun 7 PM)*

- Confirm approval before shutting down
- Stop replenishing product
- Allow station to sell down remaining product

## CLOSING PROCEDURES

*(After final ticket / station officially closed)*

### 1. Shut Down Cooking

- Turn off burners
- Remove all pots:  Water pots  Meatball pots
- Remove strainer baskets

### 2. Product Breakdown

- Properly store or discard:  Remaining sauces  Proteins  Pasta
- Label and date all saved product
- Transfer TCS items to proper refrigeration immediately

### 3. Equipment Cleaning

- Clean and sanitize:  Burners  Bains  Chaffer
- Break down and clean:  Strainers  Pots  Utensils
- Run all items through dish or send to dish

### 4. Station Breakdown

- Empty and clean:  Ice pans
- Remove and clean:  Cutting board  Knife
- Wipe and sanitize all surfaces

### 5. Floor & Trash

- Take out trash
- Sweep floors
- Mop station thoroughly

### 6. Final Reset

- Station left clean and empty
- No leftover food or debris
- All equipment off
- All product stored properly
- Check with chef before leaving

## Closing Standards (Non-Negotiable)

Do NOT break down station before approval

Do NOT run out of product before close

All TCS items must be properly cooled and stored

Station must be fully cleaned, not partially wiped

Floors must be swept and mopped

No equipment left dirty overnight

Turn on stove burners.

Place sauce pot on burner and begin heating sauce base.

Turn on range hoods flipping MUA and Fans on and the light to on.

## Check Banquets and Events

Review the day’s banquets, takeouts, and large orders.

Verify expected volume with chef or manager.

Plan sauce and meatball production accordingly.

## Station Setup

- Sauce base
- Meatballs
- Rigatoni (for backup/support)
- Containers for quarts and pints
- Utensils and pans

Ensure station is clean and organized before setup.

## Sauce Production

Make Meat Sauce:

Use prepared sauce base from prep.

Add water to achieve proper consistency.

Heat sauce fully.

Stir thoroughly using mixing tool to ensure smooth consistency.

Load sauce into sauce jack once heated.

Maintain sauce by stirring regularly.

## Meatball Setup

Pull meatballs and stock using FIFO.

Set up:

- 3 pots weekday
- 4 pots weekend

Ensure meatballs are heating and reach proper temperature before service.

Keep backup meatballs ready if needed.

## Pasta & Support Setup

Ensure awareness of pasta levels for spoon station.

Be prepared to:

- Drop rigatoni when needed
- Retrieve specialty pastas from cooler (whole wheat, GF, pappardelle, etc.)

## Lasagna & Manicotti Setup

(Active during high-volume periods)

Weekdays: begin around 4pm

Weekends: begin at open

Coordinate with hoagie bench for pans.

Set up chaffer pans when needed.

Do not overpull—replace based on expected volume.

## Utensils & Tools

Gather and set:

- Ladles for sauce
- Spoons for portioning
- Tongs (including meatball tongs)
- Mixing tools for sauce

Ensure all tools are clean and in consistent placement.

## Rail Awareness

Monitor ticket rail throughout shift.

When lasagna or manicotti pans are low:

- Count tickets on rail
- Pull correct amount for replacement
- Send pan to hoagie bench for melt

## Final Pre-Service Check

Ensure:

- Sauce is hot and at proper consistency
- Sauce jack is filled based on expected volume
- Meatballs are hot and fully stocked
- Station is clean and organized
- Tools are in place

Confirm readiness with:

- Spoon station
- Sauté station
- Hoagie bench

## Opening Standard

Station must be fully ready before service begins.

No sauce production, meatball setup, or critical prep should occur during active service.

## Notes

- Sauce jack supports the entire line—stay ahead of demand
- Spoon and sauté should not leave their stations

## Sauce Jack Closing SOP

**Prepared for:** Kitchen Staff Training

### Purpose:

Ensure the Sauce Jack station is properly reduced, cleaned, and reset at the end of service to maintain product quality, minimize waste, and prepare the station for the next shift.

A consistent closing process supports faster openings, maintains food safety standards, and ensures the kitchen remains organized and ready for continued service.

## Breakdown and Closing Procedures

### Pre-Closing:

Consolidate sauce in sauce jack based on business volume:

- 1 hour to close → reduce to 1/2 jack
- 30 minutes to close → reduce to 1/3 jack

Stir sauce regularly to maintain consistency and prevent burning.

Consolidate meatballs using FIFO. Reduce number of pots as volume slows while maintaining enough for service.

Ensure enough meatballs remain to finish service.

Monitor lasagna and manicotti pans (if active).

Count tickets on rail before pulling replacement pans. Do not overpull product late in service.

Take any unused utensils and excess pots to dish.

Organize station and remove clutter.

Wipe down surfaces (sauce jack exterior, surrounding areas) to assist with closing.

Stock containers (quarts, pints, lids) for remaining service.

Continue supporting sauté and spoon as needed while reducing unnecessary movement.

Put water on to boil for mop bucket if needed.

### Closing:

Confirm with expo and kitchen that all tickets are complete before beginning full breakdown.

Turn off sauce jack, burners, and holding equipment. Allow to cool before cleaning.

Remove remaining sauce from sauce jack and transfer to clean containers. Label and date all sauce. Store properly. Discard any unusable product.

Consolidate and store meatballs properly. Cover, label, and date. Discard any unusable product.

Remove all lasagna and manicotti pans from service. Cover and store or return to designated areas. Coordinate with hoagie bench if needed.

Break down and clean sauce jack completely.

Send all pots, utensils, and tools to dish.

Wipe down all stainless steel surfaces, including sauce jack, burners, and surrounding areas.

Clean walls, backsplash, and any buildup areas.

Remove trash and replace liners.

Sweep entire station area, including under equipment.

Prepare mop bucket with hot water and degreaser. Mop floors thoroughly.

Pull mats and place in designated dish area if applicable.

### Final Steps:

Ensure all product is properly stored and labeled.

Restock containers and basic supplies for next shift.

Notify chef of any low stock items or issues.

Confirm station is clean, organized, and fully reset.

## Notes

Maintain FIFO at all times.

Do not overproduce late in service.

Do not break down early and compromise service.

A strong close ensures faster openings and smoother service.

Opening sets the tone for the entire service.

A properly opened station results in:

- Faster ticket times
- Fewer mistakes
- Better communication
- Smoother service flow

Failure to open correctly will negatively impact the entire kitchen.

### Start-Up Procedures

1. Turn on Equipment
- Get the steam table hot.
- Turn the second and third knobs to turn 5. Turn the knob furthest to the right halfway so the flat part is straight north to south.
1. Cook meatballs
  1. Assemble pots
- There are four total meatball pots.
- Check that none are sitting in cooler 1 from the night before.
- Fill the correct number of pots with meatballs depending on daily need
- One pan of balls per pot
- Fill each pot with water two inches below the top of each pot
  1. Stove operation
- Meatballs will cook on the stove behind the spoon station.
- You will always start with four pots in the morning.
- Pots will be placed on the second, third, fourth, and fifth back burners going left to right.
- Crank heat up all the way until boiling, then reduce to low-medium heat for an hour, then shut off.
1. Water Pots
- You will always start with two water pots, except for special high-volume occasions where you may use three.
- Grab your water pots from the back pot rack. They’re large, roughly five-gallon pots.
- Fill them with water and place on the first two front burners going left to right in front of the spoon station.
1. Station Setup and Utensil Gathering
  1. General Utensils
- 1 medium sized ladle for the sauce jack
- 2 rubber spatulas
- A stack of several Bains
- 1 large ladle for meatballs
- 1 small oval serving dish for placing frequently used utensils
- Sauce spoon (typically sitting on shelf on spoon station)
- 1 large bain for stacking strainers
  1. Vermicelli
- 1 colander to be placed in the spoon sink
- 1 medium sized pot with stem handle
- 1 strainer
  1. Gluten Free
- Usually already cleaned and assembled on top shelf at the end of station.
- One small pot with stem handle
- One small strainer
  1. Pan Setup
- 2 chaffers (1 for lasagna and 1 for manicotti)
- 2 four-inch-deep hotel pans
- 2 metal spatulas
- 4 sternos
  1. Setup Plates
- From Right to Left
      1. Large Bowls (1 stack)
      1. Medium Bowls (1 stack)
      1. Rav Plates/Off White with Green Stripe (1 stack in front)
      1. Baked Pasta Plates/Older Off White with Green Strip (1 stack in back)
      1. Regular Pasta Plates (5 stacks)
  1. Setup Takeout Containers
- Foil Round Containers with Lids (1 stack each)
- 9-inch Black Bowl containers with Lids (2 stacks each)
- 7-inch Black Bowl containers with Lids (2 stacks each)
- Quart containers
- Pint Containers
- Quart/Pint Lids
1. Sauce and Sauce Jack
  1. Sauce Mixing
- Retrieve a pot of sauce base from cooler 1
      1. Sauces sit on the second shelf from the bottom at 10 o clock when entering cooler 1
      1. Always take from the right first as sauces rotate with the newest on the left and oldest moving right.
- Plug in Sauce Jack
- Add half a pot of sauce base to the jack
- Add 3 small pots of water or fill with water until 3 inches from the top
- Mix with medium ladle as sauce jack heats mixture
- Mix until smooth and heat until 160 degrees Fahrenheit
- Have chef check for consistency
  1. Dispensing Sauce
- Grab a bain from your stack
- Place under the jack spout and slowly lean the jack forward with the knob stem
- Fill just above the first indention 2 inches below the top
  1. Sauce Quantity
- Monday through Thursday fill two bains
- Friday through Sunday fill three bains
- Place filled bains into the steam well openings
- Once finished dispensing fill remainder of jack with base and water ratio until full and mix and heat until required consistency and temperature is achieved
1. Check for banquet sheets and Call-Aheads
- Check the banquet sheets hanging either on takeout or on the wall by Hoagie Bench for Spoon dishes/pans
- Check Takeout for other orders placed in advance
- Begin making pans half an hour before they’re due, or 45 minutes to an hour before if volume requires.

- Make sure all pasta bins (rigatoni, spaghetti, whole wheat) are covered for next shift
- Ensure all pasta is clean, dry, and properly stored

**Station Organization**

- Remove unused containers, clutter, and unnecessary tools
- Reset station layout for efficient closing
- Maintain clean working lanes (pasta / sauce / plating areas)

**Cleaning (Ongoing)**

- Wipe all surfaces between tickets
- Keep sauce wells clean and stirred
- Replace towels and sanitizer as needed

**Communication**

Notify closing chef of:

- Low sauces
- Low pasta
- Low meatballs
- Communicate any issues with middle, sauté, or hoagie bench

## Closing:

- Confirm all tickets are completed before full breakdown
- Communicate with expo and kitchen before shutting down station

**Equipment Shutdown**

- Turn off all burners, pasta water, and sauce jack
- Allow equipment to cool safely before cleaning

**Product Breakdown & Storage**

- Remove all sauces from sauce jack
- Transfer to clean containers, label, and date all items
- Store all sauces properly in designated areas
- Consolidate and store meatballs following food safety standards
- Discard any unusable or contaminated product

**Cleaning**:

- Pasta Pots to dish
- Meatball Pots to dish
- Strainers to dish
- Ladles to dish
- Utensils to dish
- Steam table inserts to dish
- Break down and clean sauce jack completely
- Wipe and sanitize all station surfaces
- Clean walls, backsplash, and surrounding areas

**Floors & Trash**

- Remove all trash and replace liners
- Ensure line is swept
- Ensure floors are mopped

**Restocking for Next Service**

- Ensure takeout containers are stocked
- Ensure that all pasta pans are covered in cooler
- Verify that meatballs that are being kept are properly covered with saved meatball water and plastic wrap.

**Final Check & Reporting**

Report to manager or chef:

- Low inventory
- Equipment issues
- Product concerns
- Confirm station is fully reset and ready for next service

## Notes:

- Always maintain FIFO
- Do not break down early and compromise service
- Keep station clean and organized throughout shift
- Closing is preparation for the next shift, not just cleanup
- A strong close ensures:
- Faster openings
- Better service flow
- Consistent product quality

## Hoagie and Pizza Bench SOPs

**Prepared for:** Kitchen Staff Training

## Breakdown and Closing Procedures

### Pre-Closing:

1. Obtain pans from the dish room and transfer cold rail product to new pans.
1. Take to dish any utensils and pans that are no longer needed for service.
1. Wipe down the front, sides, and top of the oven.
1. Arrange the oven screens by size (i.e. Small, Medium, Large)
1. Wipe down any services that will assist in easier cleaning at close.
1. Stock the hoagie bench with pizza boxes, buns, pizza crusts, takeout boxes, etc.
1. Put water on to boil in the prep area for mop bucket.

Closing:

1. Pull all pans from the cold rail and store in the low boy underneath the station.
1. Turn off the cold rail, steam table, grill, and turn down temp of the top oven to 400 and turn it off – bottom oven should not be turned off only turned to 0 degrees.
1. Start with cleaning the inside and top of the hoagie bench cold rail. Making sure to remove all sauce and items from inside the well itself. Wipe down cutting boards and set to the side. Finish wiping down all stainless areas and replace the cutting boards when done.
1. Pull the hoagie meat and any meatballs that are left from the steam table and dispose of the product. Turn off the steam table and open the gate valves underneath to drain it.
1. Next continue with cleaning the flattop grill using a 1/6 pan to scoop oil from the fryer. Pour oil on the flattop and use a grill brick to scour the surface. Use water to flush the flattop and scrape clean with bench scraper. Take the stainless steel surround off the flattop and use sanitizer water and a Stainless Steel scrubber to clean it. Return to the flattop and use lemon juice to finish off the grill. Replace the surround back on the flattop.
1. After that we will use the same sanitizer water and stainless steel scrubber to clean all the areas of the front of the grill moving onto the steam table.
1. Finish by wiping down all stainless steel areas.
1. Pull the mats from the line and place in the designated area in the dish room.
1. Begin sweeping the line.
1. Put hot water in mop bucket and fill the rest of the mop bucket with degreaser cleaner from mop sink room.
1. Notify Chef of Low Stock: Inform the chef in charge of any low stock items that need ordered.
1. Empty and Replace Trash Bins: Ensure all trash bins are emptied and replaced with fresh liners.
1. Deep Clean (As Needed):
  1. Utilize rags and scrubbers for thorough cleaning.
  1. Retrieve sanitizing solution and water for sanitation.

### Notes

- **Missing Service Procedures**: This document lacks procedures for assembling and cooking hoagies, pizzas, lasagna, and manicotti during service. If the “Hoagie Checklist” or additional details are provided, these can be incorporated.
- **Best Practices**: Always rotate lasagna and hoagie meat to ensure quality, as emphasized in training materials.

# App Station – Position Overview

## Overview

The App Station is responsible for the preparation and execution of all hot appetizer items during service. This station operates primarily on weekends and high-volume days and is located on the back line.

The station utilizes a broiler oven, fryer, and a sterno-held bain of meat sauce (“juice”) to execute appetizers quickly and consistently.

All Zeppole dough is prepped in advance by the prep team.

All wings are fried and sauced according to customer request.

## Key Responsibilities

### Food Preparation:

- Prepare Small and Large Bruschetta.
- Fry cheese sticks (4 for sub order, 6 for full order).
- Fry wings to requested quantity.
- Prepare Garlic Mozz Toast.
- Fry Zeppole (10 per order).
- Maintain meat sauce (“juice”) at proper holding temperature.

### Ticket Coordination:

- Monitor app tickets continuously.
- Prioritize dine-in orders when necessary.
- Confirm wing quantities before frying.
- Communicate with expo regarding large or special orders.

### Ingredient Management:

Maintain proper mise en place:

Cold Well / Ice Setup

- ½ pan bruschetta mix
- 1/6 pan mozzarella balls
- 1/6 pan Kalamata olives

Dry / Garnish

- Parsley (pint)
- Oregano (pint)

Quart Containers

- Pesto
- Sugar
- Salt/pepper mix

Bottles

- Balsamic glaze
- Oil squeeze bottle

Hot Items

- Meat sauce bain over sterno
- Melted butter
- Shredded cheese
- Sliced brick cheese
- Cut bread

Backups

- 1 pan bruschetta backup
- Wings
- Wing Sauces
- Cheese sticks
- Berries for Zeppole

### Production Standards

Bruschetta

- Small: 4 olives, 2 mozz balls
- Large: 8 olives, 4 mozz balls
- Toast base: garlic butter + pesto + brick cheese
- Broil
- Finish with oil, balsamic glaze, and parsley

Cheese Sticks

- 4 pieces (sub)
- 6 pieces (full)
- Serve with side of meat sauce (“juice”)

Wings

- Fry to order
- Sauce provided from front unless otherwise specified

Garlic Mozz Toast

- Garlic butter
- Shredded Mozz
- Broil until melted
- Sprinkle oregano on top

Zeppole

- Fry 10 per order
- Sprinkle powdered sugar on top of Zeppole
- Plate with monkeydishes of raspberry syrup, chocolate syrup, 2 strawberries (sliced) and Blueberries

### Cleaning:

- Maintain clean fryer area during service.
- Keep broiler free of excessive buildup.
- Wipe surfaces frequently.
- Follow full closing sanitation procedures.

### Inventory Management:

- Maintain par levels during service.
- Rotate product using FIFO.
- Notify management when low on wings, cheese sticks, or bruschetta mix.
- Monitor meat sauce level throughout shift.

## Shift Expectations

### Punctuality:

Arrive on time and begin full station setup immediately.

### Efficiency:

Fry and broil items promptly while maintaining quality.

### Cleanliness:

Keep station organized and fryer area safe at all times.

### Teamwork:

Communicate clearly with expo, front of house, and neighboring stations. Assist when caught up.

# Service: App Station

#### Position: App Station

#### Purpose

Maintain consistent, high-volume appetizer production during service while supporting overall kitchen flow and guest satisfaction.

Ensure fryer timing, broiler execution, and plating consistency are maintained at all times.

## Pre-Service Setup (Before Rush)

Review prep and station readiness

- Confirm cold well is stocked (bruschetta mix, mozzarella balls, olives).
- Confirm backup bruschetta pan available.
- Verify pesto, salt, salt/pepper mix stocked.
- Refill oil and balsamic glaze bottles.
- Confirm wings staged and ready.
- Confirm cheese sticks staged.
- Confirm Zeppole dough staged.
- Confirm meat sauce (“juice”) hot and holding properly.
- Stock cut bread, shredded cheese, brick cheese.
- Ensure soufflé cups stocked.
- Sanitize surfaces.

## Station Responsibilities

### Order Management

- Monitor appetizer tickets continuously.
- Confirm wing quantity before dropping in fryer.
- Prioritize dine-in tickets when necessary.
- Communicate delays to expo immediately.
- Confirm large orders before firing.

### Production

- Follow portion standards:
  - Bruschetta Small: 4 olives, 2 mozz balls.
  - Bruschetta Large: 8 olives, 4 mozz balls.
  - Cheese Sticks: 4 (sub) or 6 (full).
  - Zeppole: 10 per order.
- Fry wings until fully cooked and crispy.
- Fry cheese sticks until golden brown.
- Broil bruschetta toast and garlic mozz toast until cheese is melted and lightly golden.
- Maintain clean plating and correct garnishing.
- Double-check ramekin of meat sauce with cheese sticks.

### Team Support

- Communicate with expo during high volume.
- Notify Dessert Station when Zeppole are ready.
- Assist nearby stations if caught up.
- Request support if fryer becomes overloaded.

## Rush Procedures

- Maintain full mise en place at all times.
- Monitor fryer capacity and avoid overloading baskets.
- Rotate cold well items using FIFO.
- Call refires immediately if needed.
- Stay organized and work clean under pressure.

## Quality & Consistency

- Maintain correct portion counts on all items.
- Ensure bruschetta receives correct olive and mozzarella counts.
- Ensure balsamic glaze is applied cleanly.
- Confirm meat sauce portion with every cheese stick order.
- Maintain proper fryer temperature at 350 degrees.
- Monitor bread quality before broiling.

## End-of-Service Breakdown

- Consolidate wings and cheese sticks using FIFO.
- Transfer excess bruschetta mix to backup container.
- Wipe squeeze bottles.
- Turn off broiler and fryer following shutdown procedure.
- Remove and store meat sauce.
- Break down cold well.
- Clean fryer baskets.
- Clean broiler rack with grill brush on grate and scrape undergrates if needed.
- Sanitize station.
- Restock for next service if applicable.

## Closing Coordination

- Update par sheet.
- Report low inventory to manager.
- Report equipment issues immediately.
- Confirm next-day readiness.
- Follow Closing SOP.

# Bread & Dessert Station Position Overview

## Overview

The Bread & Dessert Station is responsible for the preparation, presentation, organization, and sanitation of all desserts and bread support during service.

This position ensures consistent plating standards, accurate portioning, proper product handling, and full station readiness for both opening and closing shifts.

All desserts are pre-made with the exception of cannoli cream, which is prepared in-house as needed. The station also verifies bread levels supplied by Hoagie Bench and supports daytime bread production when required.

## Key Responsibilities

### Food Preparation:

- Cut and prepare tiramisu (3 x 4 pattern, 2 pans daily).
- Cut and prepare Italian almond cake (2 pans daily; 1 box = 2 pans).
- Prepare cannoli cream as needed.
- Maintain gluten-free product integrity and prevent cross-contact.
- Ensure all desserts meet plating standards before leaving the station.

### Ticket Coordination:

- Execute dessert tickets promptly and accurately.
- Follow plating standards:
  - 6–7 syrup passes, back-and-forth only.
  - Dual syrups applied in opposite directions.
  - Standard whipped cream piping: front and one side.
  - Cheesecake: standard piping plus one large top dollop.
  - Chocolate cake: scallop piping plus one scoop of vanilla ice cream.
  - Gluten-free cake: no toppings.
- Use proper dishware for each dessert.
- Communicate clearly with kitchen staff when necessary.

### Ingredient Management:

- Maintain proper par levels of all cakes and pies.
- Monitor whipped cream, syrups, powdered sugar, and ice cream levels.
- Prepare and label cannoli cream properly.
- Ensure syrup bottles are filled and clean.

### Banquet Support:

- Prepare dessert trays or pans as directed.
- Assist with dessert setup for events when required.
- Coordinate timing with kitchen staff to ensure smooth service.

### Stock Rotation:

- Follow proper FIFO (First In, First Out) procedures.
- Rotate cakes and product as needed.
- Label and date cannoli cream and any newly opened items.

### Cleaning:

- Maintain a clean and organized station throughout the shift.
- Complete full pre-closing and closing procedures.
- Sanitize all food-contact surfaces nightly.
- Sweep and mop floors at close.

### Inventory Management:

- Update par sheet accurately at end of shift.
- Notify management of low product levels.
- Track waste when applicable.
- Ensure adequate product for next service.

## Shift Expectations

### Punctuality:

Arrive on time for your scheduled shift and begin opening duties promptly.

### Efficiency:

Prepare dessert tickets accurately and without delay while maintaining plating standards.

### Cleanliness:

Maintain a clean and organized workspace at all times. Station must be inspection-ready at closing.

### Teamwork:

Communicate with Hoagie Bench regarding bread levels. Assist other kitchen staff when service volume requires.

## CANNOLI CREAM – RICOTTA & MASCARPONE

### Yield

Approximately 6 lbs finished cream  
 (About 30–35 filled cannoli depending on portion)

## Ingredients

| **Ingredient** | **Quantity** | **Unit** |
|---|---|---|
| Whole Milk Ricotta (well-drained) | 4 | lb |
| Mascarpone Cheese | 2 | lb |
| Powdered Sugar | 1.25 | lb |
| Pure Vanilla Extract | 1 | tbsp |
| Fine Salt | ½ | tsp |

## Preparation Steps

### 1. Drain Ricotta

- Place ricotta in cheesecloth-lined strainer.
- Drain minimum 4–6 hours (overnight preferred).
- Remove as much moisture as possible.

This step determines final texture.

### 2. Mix Base

1. In large mixing bowl, combine drained ricotta and mascarpone.
1. Mix until smooth and fully incorporated.
1. Add powdered sugar gradually.
1. Mix just until smooth — do not overwhip.

### 3. Flavor

- Add vanilla extract.
- Add fine salt.
- Mix gently until combined.

### 4. Texture Check

Finished cream should be:

- Thick
- Smooth
- Pipeable
- Able to hold shape when piped

If too loose:

- Add small amount powdered sugar.

If too stiff:

- Add 1–2 tablespoons heavy cream and mix gently.

### 5. Storage

- Transfer to labeled container.
- Date and refrigerate.
- Keep tightly covered.
- Fill piping bags as needed for service.

**Position:** Dishwasher  
 **Shift:** Lunch / Dinner

## Purpose

Maintain a continuous flow of clean dishes, cookware, and utensils while supporting all kitchen and front-of-house operations through proper cleaning, organization, and sanitation.

## Core Responsibility

- Keep dish flow always moving
- Prevent backups at all stations
- Ensure all items are properly cleaned, sanitized, and stored
- Maintain cleanliness of dish room, kitchen, and prep areas

## Dish Room Structure

### 1. Loader (pre-rinse)

- Scrape, spray, and prep all dishes before machine
- Remove all food debris (machine has no pre-rinse cycle)
- Ensure racks are properly loaded
- Do NOT send dirty dishes through

### 2. Machine (Washer/Catcher)

**Catcher Responsibilities:**

- Pull racks from machine
- Check cleanliness
- Re-run if needed
- Sort items for storage

### 3. 3-Bowl Sink (Pots & Pans)

- **Wash → Rinse → Sanitize** all:  Pots  Pans  Server trays
- Scrub thoroughly before sending through machine if needed

### 4. Runner (Flow Control)

- Pick up dirty dishes from:  Side station  Middle station
- **Timing standard:Slow → every 30 minutesBusy → every 10–15 minutes**
- Prevent pileups before they happen

## Additional Responsibilities

- Clean all mats (front + back line) through dish machine
- Prep mats sprayed off outside before washing
- Put away all clean items:  Dishes  Glasses  Silverware  Pots/pans  Utensils
- Separate silverware for rolling
- Sweep and mop:  Dish room  Kitchen  Prep area

## Flow Standard

- Dishes should never sit and pile up
- Machine should never stop running during service
- Clean items should not sit—put them away immediately

## Cleaning Standard

- All dishes must be fully clean before leaving dish
- No food debris
- No grease
- No water spots where avoidable

## Non-Negotiables

- No dirty dishes go through machine
- No standing around while dishes are backed up
- No leaving dishes for next shift
- Floors must be fully cleaned nightly
- Mats must be washed daily

## Core Principle

**Stay ahead of the dish, don’t chase it**

## Dish Pit Emergency System (When slammed)

## Purpose

Keep dish flow from collapsing during peak volume by immediately adjusting roles and priorities.

Switch to this system when:

- Dishes are stacking at stations
- Machine can’t keep up
- Pots and pans are backing up
- Clean dishes are not being put away fast enough

**If you’re asking, “are we slammed?” - you already are**

**Dishes > Everything else**

Stop:

- extra cleaning
- organizing
- anything not directly tied to dish flow

- Focus ONLY on:

- Keep constant flow into machine

- Pull racks immediately
- Quick check (don’t over-inspect)

- Skip unnecessary soaking delays
- Keep items moving back to kitchen fast

**Survive the rush first, clean up after**

title: Health Inspection Awareness Class Script
body:
# Muriale’s Health Inspection Success Program

## Class Script

**Suggested class time:** 35–45 minutes  
 **Audience:** Kitchen, prep, dish/stewarding, sous chefs, managers/PICs  
 **Trainer:** Kitchen Operations Manager / Chef  
 **Goal:** Teach employees how their everyday actions affect food safety and inspection performance.

# Slide 1 — Muriale’s Health Inspection Success Program

### Script

“Today we’re going over our Health Inspection Success Program.

The first thing I want everyone to understand is that this is **not a program about cleaning up because we think the health department is coming.**

That is exactly what I do not want.

The goal is for this kitchen to operate every day in a condition where, if an inspector walked through that door right now, we would be ready.

That means inspection readiness becomes part of how we cook, prep, receive trucks, wash dishes, store food, clean, and close the kitchen.

There are five basic ideas behind everything we’re going to talk about today:

**Hygiene first. Control temperatures. Follow the system. Clean and sanitize correctly. Train and help each other.**

If we do those things consistently, better inspection scores are going to follow naturally.

But the real reason we do them is simpler: **safe food, safe employees, and safe guests.**”

### Ask the room

“Who is responsible for food safety in this kitchen?”

Let them answer.

“The answer is **everybody**. Management has additional responsibilities, but food safety does not belong to one manager.”

# Slide 2 — Program Goals & Success Standards

### Script

“This program has six main goals.

First, **we stay inspection-ready every day.**

Second, we want to prevent critical violations before they happen.

Third, if something is wrong, we correct it immediately instead of walking past it.

Fourth, we protect our guests and ourselves.

Fifth, everybody gets trained on the standards that apply to their job.

And sixth, we keep enough documentation to prove that we are actually managing food safety.

When I say ‘what good looks like,’ I’m talking about things you should be able to see immediately:

A hand sink is stocked and accessible.

Temperatures are correct.

Food has a date and initials on it.

Sanitizer is mixed correctly.

Food is stored correctly.

Records are filled out.

None of those things are complicated. The challenge is doing them **every shift, every day.**”

### Teaching point

“Most inspection problems are not caused because nobody knows the rule. They happen because the standard slowly slips.”

# Slide 3 — Daily Inspection Routine

### Script

“This is where the program actually works.

We are using three levels of daily verification: **opening, mid-shift, and closing.**

At opening, we are asking: **Are we ready to operate safely?**

Are the hand sinks stocked?

Are the walk-ins and coolers running correctly?

Are temperatures good?

Is sanitizer set up?

Are foods dated and rotated?

Are thermometers available?

During service, the questions change.

Now we are watching what people are actually doing.

Are hands being washed?

Are gloves being changed?

Are hot and cold foods staying at temperature?

Are raw foods being kept away from ready-to-eat foods?

Are sanitizer buckets and wiping cloths being handled correctly?

Are people cleaning as they go?

Then at closing we are protecting tomorrow.

Food has to be cooled correctly.

Everything needs labels and dates.

Old food gets discarded.

Food-contact surfaces get cleaned and sanitized.

Trash gets controlled.

And if something is wrong, we document it instead of leaving it for somebody else to discover tomorrow.”

### Ask

“What is easier — fixing a missing date mark when we see it or explaining twenty unlabeled containers to an inspector?”

# Slide 4 — Weekly Self-Inspection System

### Script

“In addition to daily checks, once a week we do a full self-inspection.

This is supposed to feel like an inspection.

We walk the whole operation, not just the easy areas.

We use the checklist.

We score what we actually see.

If we find a problem that keeps coming back, we flag it as a repeat issue.

Then somebody gets assigned to fix it, with a deadline.

And finally, we verify that it was actually fixed.

That last part matters.

Writing ‘fixed’ on a form does not fix anything.

If a cooler gasket is damaged, we verify the repair.

If an employee keeps storing raw product incorrectly, we verify that the behavior changed.

If sanitizer is repeatedly being mixed wrong, we retrain and then check it again.

**What gets inspected gets improved.**”

# Slide 5 — Critical Focus Areas, Part 1

### Employee Health & Hygiene

“First is employee health.

If you are vomiting, have diarrhea, jaundice, fever with sore throat, or certain infected wounds or sores, you need to tell management.

Do not decide for yourself that it is probably fine.

Tell us.

We would much rather solve a staffing problem than create a foodborne-illness problem.”

### Hand Sinks & Handwashing

“Hand sinks are for handwashing. They are not storage shelves, dump sinks, thawing sinks, or places for towels and utensils.

They need soap, paper towels, water, and clear access.

And gloves do not replace handwashing.”

### Temperature Control

“Our basic holding numbers are easy to remember:

**Cold: 41°F or below.Hot: 135°F or above.**

Reheating TCS foods for hot holding means getting them to the required reheating temperature quickly.

And if we are cooking something that requires a specific internal temperature, we use a thermometer. We don't guess.”

### Date Marking & FIFO

“At Muriale’s, we keep this simple.

One strip of masking tape.

**Date and initials.**

That’s it.

Then FIFO: older product goes where it gets used first.

If I have to move three new pans to find an old pan hiding in the back, FIFO is not being followed.”

### Cross-Contamination

“Raw and ready-to-eat stay separated.

That means storage, cutting boards, knives, utensils, hands, gloves, and prep surfaces.

One dirty knife can undo everything we did correctly before it.”

# Slide 6 — Critical Focus Areas, Part 2

### Cleaning & Sanitizing

“Cleaning and sanitizing are not the same thing.

**Cleaning removes food and soil. Sanitizing reduces microorganisms to a safe level.**

For food-contact equipment, the basic sequence is:

**Wash. Rinse. Sanitize. Air dry.**

You cannot sanitize through a layer of grease or food.”

### Storage & Receiving

“Receiving is our first opportunity to stop bad product from entering the building.

When a truck arrives, we are checking product temperature, packaging, condition, frozen product, expiration, shortages, substitutions, and whether the product is actually acceptable.

Once product is inside, food stays protected, covered when appropriate, off the floor, and separated from chemicals.”

### Facility & Equipment

“An inspector does not only look at food.

They look at leaks, floors, drains, walls, ceilings, ventilation, damaged equipment, refrigeration, plumbing, and whether our equipment is clean and in good repair.

If something is broken, report it. Do not just learn how to work around it.”

### Pests, Garbage & Chemicals

“Food debris, standing water, open doors, overflowing trash, and dirty dumpster areas attract pests.

Chemicals need to be labeled and stored correctly.

And one rule everybody should remember:

**Never mix chemicals.**

If you are unsure what something is or how to use it, stop and ask.”

### PIC Knowledge, Records & Training

“Finally, an inspector wants to see whether management is actually managing food safety.

Can we explain what we're doing?

Can employees explain what applies to their jobs?

And do our records support what we're saying?”

# Slide 7 — Corrective Action Workflow

### Script

“This may be the most important management slide in the class.

When we find a problem, we use the same basic process every time.

**Spot it.Protect people and food.Correct it.Document it when necessary.Assign follow-up.Verify it.Retrain if needed.**

Here is an example.

We find chicken sitting above safe temperature.

We do not write it down and keep walking.

First, we protect the food and determine whether it is safe.

Then we determine why the temperature is wrong.

Did the cooler fail?

Was the door left open?

Was it just put away hot?

Was it sitting out?

Then we correct the cause.

If maintenance is involved, we create the work order.

If someone needs coaching, we coach them.

Then we verify that the problem is actually gone.”

### Key line

“**Corrective action is not punishment. It is how we keep a small mistake from becoming a large problem.**”

# Slide 8 — Training & Coaching System

### Script

“Training is not something we do once when somebody gets hired and then forget about.

New hires need the basics.

After that, most training should happen in the kitchen.

If I see something wrong, I would rather correct it right there while the employee is doing the job.

That is coaching.

We also have toolbox talks, training images, posters, and signoffs.

If the same problem keeps happening, that tells us something.

Either the employee doesn't understand the standard, the process is poorly designed, supervision is weak, or the equipment/setup is making the correct behavior difficult.

We need to find out which one.”

### Ask

“If three different people make the same mistake, is it automatically three bad employees?”

“No. At that point, we also need to look at the system.”

# Slide 9 — Inspection Day Game Plan

### Script

“Now let's talk about the day an actual inspector arrives.

Number one: **do not panic.**

We do not start running around the kitchen hiding things or creating chaos.

The Person in Charge gets notified.

One knowledgeable manager should accompany the inspector when appropriate.

If an inspector asks you something you know, answer it.

If you do not know the answer, do not make something up.

Say you don't know and get the manager.

If we can correct something safely and appropriately during the inspection, we correct it.

We take notes on findings.

We keep normal safe operations running.

And when the inspection is over, management reviews the report and makes sure every follow-up item is assigned.”

### Strong line

“The best inspection-day strategy is having done the work for the previous 364 days.”

# Slide 10 — Monthly Review & Accountability

### Script

“Once a month, I don't just want to look at one inspection score.

I want to know what the scores are telling us.

What keeps showing up?

Are we repeatedly missing date marks?

Are temperature issues happening on one shift?

Does the same piece of equipment keep creating sanitation problems?

Are corrective actions being completed?

Do we have training gaps?

Do we need to change an SOP, storage location, par, piece of equipment, or supervision?

The goal is continuous improvement.

If we keep seeing the same problem month after month, then filling out another checklist is not enough.

Something in the operation needs to change.”

# Slide 11 — Scoring & Severity System

### Script

“Our internal scoring system gives us a way to measure ourselves consistently.

This is **our internal management score**. It is not the health department's official scoring formula.

A compliant item costs us nothing.

If we find something and correct it on the spot, that is a small deduction because the program did its job — we found it and fixed it.

A major finding is worth a larger deduction.

A critical finding is the most serious because it can immediately affect food safety or employee safety.

Examples of critical issues would include things like unsafe temperatures, serious cross-contamination, lack of handwashing capability, sewage problems, illness-control failures, or active contamination.

Our target is:

**95–100: Green.90–94: Yellow.Below 90: Red.**

And an unresolved critical issue is a serious failure regardless of the overall number.

The purpose is not to chase a number.

The score lets us compare week to week and see whether the kitchen is getting stronger or weaker.”

# Slide 12 — Records & Documentation

### Script

“There is an old saying in food safety:

**If it isn't documented, it didn't happen.**

That doesn't mean paperwork is more important than actually doing the job.

It means the records prove we are managing the job.

We maintain things like:

Temperature records.

Cleaning and sanitation records.

Corrective-action records.

Training records.

Inspection records.

Maintenance and work-order records.

Vendor and pest-service records.

Health department reports.

An inspector should be able to see that food safety at Muriale’s is not random.

There is a system behind it.”

### Example

“If a cooler had a problem last month, I want to be able to show:

We found it.

We protected the food.

We put in the work order.

It was repaired.

We verified the temperature.

That is active management.”

# Slide 13 — Person in Charge Responsibilities

### Script

“This slide is aimed primarily at managers, sous chefs, and anybody serving as Person in Charge, but everybody should understand what the PIC is responsible for.

The PIC needs to **know, monitor, correct, document, and train.**

The manager should be able to answer questions such as:

What are we serving today?

How are those foods cooked?

What are our important temperatures?

How do we cool food?

How do we store it?

What sanitizer are we using and what concentration should it be?

When were temperatures last checked?

What current food-safety problems do we have?

How were they corrected?

Who is responsible for what today?

The PIC cannot spend the entire shift in an office and still effectively manage food safety.

You have to be in the kitchen and actually looking at what is happening.”

# Slide 14 — 15-Minute Inspection Sweep

### Script

“This is our fast inspection sweep.

It is useful before an expected inspection or as a surprise internal drill.

It **does not replace our regular program.**

In fifteen minutes, I should be able to look at the highest-risk areas.

Hand sinks.

Temperatures.

Labels and dates.

Sanitizer.

Storage.

Floors and surfaces.

Chemicals.

Trash.

Pest evidence.

I also want to look at employee practices and whether the manager knows what is happening.

The idea is to catch obvious problems quickly.

A missing soap dispenser is easy to fix when we notice it ourselves.

A missing soap dispenser is a violation when the inspector notices it first.

Small things add up.”

# Slide 15 — Final Team Expectations

### Script

“This last slide is the part I want everybody to leave with.

**Our habits become our score.**

We take pride in our kitchen.

We follow the system even when nobody is watching.

We communicate when something is wrong.

And we improve instead of hiding mistakes.

If you see a food-safety problem, speak up.

If you do not understand something, ask.

If equipment is unsafe, stop using it and report it.

If food is unsafe, do not serve it.

If you make a mistake, correct it.

Nobody here should be afraid to point out a food-safety problem.

I would rather hear about a problem immediately than find out later that somebody knew and didn't say anything.

This program is not about making more paperwork for everybody.

It's about making sure we are doing things right often enough that **the correct way becomes the normal way.**

That protects our guests.

It protects each other.

It protects the restaurant.

And yes, when the health department comes in, it should also result in a much better inspection.”

# Class Close

I would finish the class with this:

“Before we finish, I want everybody to remember three things.

**First: if you see something wrong, do not walk past it.**

Either correct it or tell somebody who can.

**Second: food safety does not belong only to management.**

Every person who touches food, equipment, dishes, chemicals, storage, or the facility affects food safety.

**Third: we are not going to wait for an inspector to tell us how our kitchen is doing.**

We are going to inspect ourselves, correct ourselves, and improve ourselves.

That is how this program works.”

Then ask:

“Any questions about anything we covered, or anything in the kitchen you've seen that you think we need to address?”

That last question is worth asking. It turns the class from a lecture into an opportunity to identify real problems.

## After the class

Have employees sign the training record or **Chef Toolbox Talk** sheet. I would then follow the classroom session with a **10–15 minute walk through the actual kitchen**, where you physically point out:

- hand sinks,
- thermometer locations,
- sanitizer/test strips,
- date-marking examples,
- raw/RTE storage,
- chemical storage,
- inspection records,
- corrective-action location,
- equipment out-of-service/LOTO tags,
- and anything at Muriale’s that you specifically expect them to recognize.

body:
## New Hire Kitchen Orientation — Trainer Script

**Recommended classroom time:** about 30–40 minutes  
 **Then:** kitchen walk-through and hands-on training  
 **Trainer:** Kitchen Operations Manager, sous chef, or assigned kitchen trainer

## Slide 1 — New Hire Kitchen Orientation Program

“Welcome to Muriale’s.

By the time you’re sitting through this, Kim and Hire365 have already handled the hiring and HR side of things. What we’re going to cover now is the part that actually prepares you to work in our kitchen.

This orientation is about three things.

First, we’re going to teach you the basic safety and food-safety rules that apply to everybody who works back here.

Second, we’re going to teach you how **Muriale’s** does things. Every kitchen has its own systems, and there are some specific standards here that we expect everyone to follow.

Third, once the basic orientation is done, you’ll start learning your actual station and equipment. You’re not considered trained on something just because somebody mentioned it to you. You’ll have a chance to see it, practice it, and demonstrate that you can do it safely.

Nobody expects you to know the whole kitchen today. We do expect you to ask questions and follow the standards we teach you.”

## Slide 2 — How the Orientation Is Broken Up

“We do **not** try to teach you everything in one day.

Your first shift is about getting comfortable with the kitchen and learning the rules that you need immediately.

That includes knowing where things are, who you report to, handwashing, illness reporting, basic food temperatures, our date-labeling system, FIFO, and the safety rules you need before you start working.

During shifts two through five, we’ll get deeper into food storage, sanitation, chemicals, allergens, equipment safety, and the standards we use to keep the kitchen inspection-ready.

Then during roughly shifts six through ten, the focus shifts heavily toward your actual job.

You’ll be working your station, learning the equipment you use, getting coached, and eventually being signed off on the things you can perform correctly.

If something takes longer than ten shifts, that’s okay. The goal is competency, not racing through a checklist.”

## Slide 3 — First Shift: Welcome, Tour & Who to Report To

“Before you start working, you need to know how this kitchen is laid out and who you go to when you need something.

We’re going to walk you through the front line, back line, prep areas, walk-ins, freezers, dry storage, dish area, chemical storage, trash and grease areas, hand sinks, exits, first aid, and fire equipment.

You’ll also be shown where you keep personal belongings and where breaks, drinks, and employee food are handled.

One of the most important things I want you to understand is this: **if you don’t know, ask.**

We would much rather stop for thirty seconds and answer a question than have you guess with food, chemicals, or equipment.

You’ll also meet the manager on duty and your primary trainer. If you see a food-safety problem, a broken piece of equipment, an injury, a spill, or anything else that doesn’t look right, tell one of us.”

## Slide 4 — Employee Health & Hygiene

“This is something the health department takes very seriously, and so do we.

If you are vomiting, have diarrhea, jaundice, fever with a sore throat, or certain infected wounds or sores, you need to tell management.

Do not decide on your own that you’re probably okay to work around food.

Tell us what is going on and let management determine what needs to happen.

We also expect clean work clothing and proper personal hygiene.

Hair restraints are used where required, and beard restraints are used when required.

If you have a cut or wound on your hand or arm, it needs to be properly protected. If it affects food handling, there may also be a glove requirement.

The important thing is communication.

A staffing inconvenience is much easier to deal with than a foodborne illness.”

## Slide 5 — Handwashing & Glove Use

“Handwashing is one of the simplest things we do, and it is also one of the easiest ways to prevent foodborne illness.

You wash your hands before you start working and anytime they may have become contaminated.

That means after using the restroom, touching your face or hair, handling raw food, touching trash, eating, drinking, smoking, cleaning, handling chemicals, or doing anything else that can contaminate your hands.

When you wash, do it correctly. Soap, friction, and enough time matter. We train to at least twenty seconds of scrubbing.

Gloves are useful, but gloves do **not** replace handwashing.

Dirty gloves are just dirty hands with plastic over them.

Change gloves when you change tasks, when you go from raw food to ready-to-eat food, when they become dirty or torn, or anytime they become contaminated.

And our hand sinks need to stay clear. They are not storage shelves, dump sinks, or places to leave utensils.”

## Slide 6 — Temperature Control

“One of the biggest things you’re going to hear about in this kitchen is temperature.

For everyday holding, remember two numbers:

**Cold food: 41 degrees Fahrenheit or below.**

**Hot-held food: 135 degrees Fahrenheit or above.**

Cooking, cooling, and reheating have their own requirements, and we’ll train you on those as they apply to your job.

The important rule is: **use the thermometer.**

We don’t look at something and say, ‘That feels cold enough.’

We don’t guess whether chicken is done.

If temperature matters, we verify it.

The probe also needs to be clean and sanitized before and after use.

If you check something and the temperature is wrong, tell somebody immediately. Do not hide it, and do not serve food you believe may be unsafe.”

## Slide 7 — Muriale’s Date Marking & FIFO

“This is one of the Muriale’s-specific standards I want you to learn exactly the way we do it.

Our date marking is simple.

We use **one strip of masking tape**.

On that tape, put the **date and your initials**.

That’s our standard.

Then we use FIFO — First In, First Out.

Older usable product should be positioned so we use it first.

New product goes behind it.

If we keep putting new food in front of old food, eventually the old stuff gets forgotten in the back.

If you find something without a date, with a questionable date, or something you’re not sure about, don’t guess.

Bring it to a manager or trainer before you use it.

And don’t invent your own labeling system. We want everyone doing this the same way.”

## Slide 8 — Cold Storage & Cross-Contamination

“How we store food matters just as much as the temperature.

Ready-to-eat foods need to be protected from raw animal products.

That means we store foods in an order that reduces the chance that raw juices can drip or leak onto something that will not receive another cooking step.

You’ll see our cold-storage training image posted as a reference.

The same idea applies during prep.

If you work with raw chicken and then turn around and start handling ready-to-eat food with the same gloves, knife, cutting board, or dirty surface, you have created a cross-contamination risk.

Clean and sanitize between incompatible tasks.

Change gloves.

Use clean tools.

And when you are not sure whether two things can safely share a surface or utensil, stop and ask.”

## Slide 9 — Cleaning, Sanitizing & Chemical Safety

“Cleaning and sanitizing are two different things.

**Cleaning removes food, grease, and soil.**

**Sanitizing reduces microorganisms to a safe level after the surface is clean.**

For food-contact surfaces, remember the basic sequence:

**Wash. Rinse. Sanitize. Air dry.**

You cannot sanitize through a layer of food or grease.

For sanitizer, we use the correct chemical and the correct test strips.

Don’t guess whether the sanitizer is strong enough.

We test it.

If it’s dirty, weak, or outside the proper range, it gets corrected.

Chemicals must stay labeled and stored where they belong.

Follow PPE and dilution instructions.

And one rule applies to every chemical in this building:

**Never mix chemicals.**

If there is a chemical spill or exposure, stop and get management. Don’t start experimenting with cleanup chemicals.”

## Slide 10 — Kitchen Safety Basics

“A kitchen can hurt you very quickly if you get careless.

With knives, use a stable cutting board, use the right knife, and keep the handle clean and dry.

Never put knives loose in a sink where somebody can’t see them.

And if you drop a knife, let it fall. Do not try to catch it.

With hot equipment, assume something is hot until you know otherwise.

Use dry towels or proper heat protection. Be careful around steam, ovens, fryers, pans, and lids.

We also communicate when moving around the kitchen.

You’ll hear people say things like **hot, behind, and corner.**

Those calls are there for a reason. Use them.

Spills get cleaned up quickly. Walkways and exits stay clear. We don’t leave boxes, cords, tools, or other trip hazards where people are working.

And if you get hurt, report it. Even if it seems minor.”

## Slide 11 — Equipment Safety, Out-of-Service & Lockout/Tagout

“You are not automatically trained on every piece of equipment because you work in the kitchen.

If you haven’t been shown how to use something, do not use it until you’ve been trained.

Never bypass a guard, safety switch, interlock, or other safety device because it slows you down.

If equipment is sparking, leaking, overheating, making a bad noise, smells like something is burning, or simply does not seem safe, stop using it and tell management.

You may also see equipment with an **OUT OF SERVICE** tag.

That means exactly what it says.

Do not plug it back in.

Do not reset it.

Do not move the tag.

Do not see whether maybe it works now.

The same goes for **Lockout/Tagout**.

Only trained and authorized employees perform Lockout/Tagout.

If something is locked or tagged out, leave it alone.

Electrical verification or electrical repair work is not something a regular new kitchen employee should be doing.”

## Slide 12 — Allergen Awareness

“Food allergies can be life-threatening, so there is no room for guessing.

If an allergy order comes through, take it seriously and make sure the chef or manager knows about it.

If you don’t know whether an ingredient contains an allergen, don’t tell somebody you think it’s safe.

We verify.

When preparing an allergy order, we may need clean and sanitized tools, pans, utensils, surfaces, and fresh gloves.

The point is to prevent cross-contact.

Communication is extremely important because an allergy order can pass through multiple people before it reaches the guest.

If you are ever unsure, stop and ask.”

## Slide 13 — Muriale’s Operating Standards

“This slide brings together some of the things that are specific to how we expect this kitchen to operate.

First, **date tape** means one strip of masking tape with the date and initials.

Second, FIFO means older usable product first.

Third, we operate inspection-ready.

That does not mean we clean because we heard an inspector is coming.

It means we try to keep things right all the time.

If you see something broken, unsafe, or not working correctly, report it early.

Don’t wait until it completely fails.

We also clean as we go.

Don’t let spills, food debris, boxes, dirty utensils, or clutter build up around your station.

And communicate.

If we’re running low on something, say it.

If something is unsafe, say it.

If a cooler doesn’t seem right, say it.

If food looks questionable, say it.

Good kitchen communication prevents a lot of problems.”

## Slide 14 — First Week Training Plan

“This is roughly how your first week will progress.

On shift one, we concentrate on the tour, food-safety basics, illness reporting, handwashing, date marking, FIFO, and immediate safety.

On shift two, we start getting deeper into storage, temperatures, cross-contamination, thermometers, sanitizer, and test strips.

On shift three, we concentrate more on cleaning, sanitizing, chemicals, waste, pest prevention, and the dish process if it applies to your job.

On shift four, you’ll get more equipment-specific safety training, along with burns, cuts, slips, out-of-service equipment, and Lockout/Tagout awareness.

On shift five, we reinforce allergen handling, inspection-ready habits, corrective actions, documentation, and anything you’ve had questions about.

Then shifts six through ten focus primarily on your actual job.

That’s when we build station competency.

Again, this is not a race. If you need more work on something, we keep training.”

## Slide 15 — Station Competency & Final Signoff

“This is the part that actually tells us whether your orientation has worked.

Hearing me explain something does not mean you’re trained on it.

We want to see you perform the job.

Can you set up your station correctly?

Can you safely operate the equipment you are expected to use?

Can you follow our recipes, portions, and production standards?

Can you control temperatures?

Can you prevent cross-contamination?

Can you date food correctly and follow FIFO?

Can you keep your station organized and sanitary?

Can you communicate when something is running low or something is wrong?

Can you close and clean your area properly?

And most importantly, do you know when to **stop and ask for help?**

When those things are demonstrated consistently, then we sign you off.

A signoff does not mean somebody told you about the task.

It means you demonstrated that you can perform it safely and correctly.”

# Closing the Orientation

I would finish the PowerPoint with this:

“There is a lot of information here, and nobody expects you to memorize everything today.

What I do expect is that you remember the basic rules.

Wash your hands.

Keep food at safe temperatures.

Prevent cross-contamination.

Date and rotate food correctly.

Clean and sanitize properly.

Respect equipment and safety tags.

Tell us when something is wrong.

And if you don’t know, ask.

You will learn the rest by working with us over the next several shifts.

We want you to become fast and efficient, but **correct and safe comes before fast**. Once you learn the right way, speed comes with repetition.”

Then ask:

“Before we walk the kitchen, what questions do you have about anything we just covered?”

## Immediately after the PowerPoint

Take the employee on the physical kitchen tour while everything is fresh.

Show them the actual hand sinks, thermometer locations, sanitizer and test strips, cold-storage layout, masking tape/date-marking setup, chemical/SDS location, first aid, extinguishers, exits, out-of-service/LOTO tags, and the equipment on the station they’ll eventually be using. Then hand them off to the trainer responsible for training them.

title: Health Inspection Success Program
